top.line: Approve once at each altitude; lower levels only narrow
top.para: Models can draft two hundred decision policies, but no owner can sign off two hundred. Decisions sit at altitudes, from board strategy to a single run, and each level signs off once while those below inherit it. A lower level may narrow, never widen, checked against declared envelopes, as English law treats delegated powers.

in-short.line: Writing policies is cheap; signing them at altitude scales
in-short.para: A model can draft two hundred policies but no owner can approve them all, so each altitude, strategic to run, signs off once and the levels below inherit it. Lower levels may narrow, never widen, against a declared envelope checked in CI for numbers and flagged by a model for words. Delegated legislation exceeding its Act is likewise ultra vires.

problem.line: Cheap policy drafting moves the bottleneck to sign-off
problem.para: Every branch point touching money, people, irreversibility or business risk earns a decision policy, and a model can draft five, a hundred or two hundred in an afternoon. A head of support can approve five properly, not two hundred, and signing without reading is a rubber stamp: liability, not agency.

altitudes.line: Decisions sit at altitudes, each bounded by its parent
altitudes.para: Decisions form a fractal, not a flat list: strategic, signed by the board; business, by a function head; product, by a team; technical, by an engineer; and the run, by nobody or the agent. Each has its own workflows, from the annual plan to a refund's five steps. Labels vary; the bounding matters.

approve.line: Each level reads only its own, and below inherits
approve.para: The board approves a risk appetite, as the UK Corporate Governance Code's Principle O and ISO Guide 73 describe, not the refund tool. The head of support approves limits, a team its workflow, an engineer the tool. Two hundred policies at the bottom are fine if each fits inside the few approved above.

narrow.line: A lower level may narrow, never widen, its parent
narrow.para: A team may set a person-decides threshold of 50 GBP when the business said 100, but not 200. English law calls the widening ultra vires: on 26 July 2017 the Supreme Court quashed the employment tribunal fees order in R (UNISON) v Lord Chancellor, holding it "unlawful ab initio".

envelope.line: Every policy declares an envelope with the same fields
envelope.para: An envelope gives a policy's bounds: money, blast radius, data in scope, people in scope, reversibility and duration. At business level that might be automatic refunds of at most 2,000 GBP a day; at run level, one refund up to 100 GBP. Identical fields make levels comparable, so the check needs no person.

check.line: Numbers check in CI; a model flags conflicting words
check.para: With envelopes declared, numbers and lists compare deterministically in CI on every policy change. Wording conflicts are flagged by a model for a person to decide. This also finds the unpredicted: a VIP workflow refunding up to 1,000 GBP without a person must be decided at the level owning the 100 GBP limit.

kill.line: Kill switches sit with their envelope; escalate one level
kill.para: A kill switch belongs to the altitude whose envelope it protects: the 2,000 GBP daily circuit breaker stops all automatic refunds at business level. Escalation goes up one altitude to whoever owns the limits, not straight to the board. A licence to operate is a named envelope, signed off once and checkable from below.

not.line: Someone must still write a measurable top level
not.para: A vague risk appetite cannot be checked against, so the mechanical check is only as good as the top numbers. Envelopes can be gamed by splitting refunds, so aggregate limits like the daily breaker are needed. Altitude follows what is decided, not the org chart, and a model's flags on words are only suggestions.

series.line: Second of four: policies, altitude, case law, mapping
series.para: The series has four parts: Three policies for an agent, on behaviour, decision and workflow; this piece, Approve at altitude; Case law for agents, on the cases nobody predicted; and Three decisions, mapped. That last part covers the scenarios, including the refund in the figure.

limits.line: A proposal with illustrative numbers and a legal analogy
limits.para: No decision-policy format with envelopes exists yet; the fields are mine and the numbers illustrative. The tool's limits come from the third design in Hope or enforcement, the levels above are made up, and the legal parallel borrows the shape, not the authority. People signing off at these altitudes can write to agent@riskmandate.ai.

sources.line: Sources: the judgment, governance codes and site articles
sources.para: A voice memo of mine from 17 October 2026, written up by the site's agent. R (UNISON) v Lord Chancellor [2017] UKSC 51, the UK Corporate Governance Code's Principle O, ISO Guide 73:2009, the FRC's 2018 Guidance on Board Effectiveness, Hope or enforcement for the refund limits, and related site articles.
